title: Death in custody prompts questions: Family in dark about man's final hours
article: Family members of a Calgary man who died in police custody are demanding answers about the final few hours of the 27-year-old's life.

Members of Tamer Sayed Roha's family will meet city homicide investigators this week to discuss a probe into the death, but say they're uncomfortable with the fact police officers are investigating their own.

"Although the police have agreed to see us and gave us some preliminary details, there is mounting concern the truth will never come out," said Roha's aunt, who spoke on behalf of the family but asked that her name not be used.
Acting Staff Sgt. Craig Cuthbert of the homicide unit said the investigation will follow standard procedures, a practice hundreds of years old in policing.
"If there's fault to be found we'll find the fault," he said. "If not, we won't."
The family also questions why it took six hours for them to be told of Roha's death and why his face was bruised.

Roha died Wednesday night, shortly after police were called to the Quality Inn at 2359 Banff Tr. N.W. They were called to his room around 10:25 p.m. after reports a man inside was acting oddly and disturbing other hotel guests.
Upon arrival of police at the suite, Cuthbert said, Roha was behaving in a "bizarre" manner. Emergency Medical Services was called to assist, while police officers stood back.

"He was biting, gouging, spitting and kicking," Cuthbert said, adding Roha's face was scarred from rug burn while he was being placed in handcuffs to restrain him, according to a pathologist's remarks.
"When a person is completely out of control and not lucid, we try to calm them the best we can. We didn't even approach him until EMS arrived," Cuthbert said.

The day after the incident, police Staff Sgt. Bryant Petkau of the homicide unit said there did not appear to have been any criminal activity on behalf of members of the police service who were in attendance, or anyone with EMS.
Roha's aunt said her nephew was a "very quiet, shy individual" and the family is having difficulty reconciling their memories of him with Wednesday's events.

"We have questions about the police's handling of him and how he was transported to hospital," she said. The family spokeswoman also expressed concern at how long it took police to notify the family, saying that although the incident happened at about 10:35 p.m. Wednesday night, they weren't told until close to 4:30 a.m.
Cuthbert said Roha had checked into the hotel under a different name and did not have any identification on him, nor was any found in the room.
"There's always a delay in notifying next of kin," he said. "It would have been faster if he checked in under his name and carried ID."

Family members said Roha had been battling a substance abuse problem for a year and his mother had tried in vain to keep him in treatment. Roha's mother told the Herald last week she tried to force her son into drug treatment programs and even obtained a mental health warrant from the courts, but those actions didn't carry enough weight to hold and treat him against his will.
"She said today that she wouldn't wish this on her worst enemy," Roha's aunt said.
Roha's aunt said the family is considering hiring a lawyer to represent them, but added the cost is an impediment.
"We're hoping someone from the public with some sort of experience in this area will come forward," she said.
Police said no drug paraphernalia was found in Roha's room and results of toxicology reports aren't expected for three weeks.
